source_rows.content: The condition is defined by the matrix rising; stomach disturbance and weakened appetite are linked with weakness of the heart.
Fainting and an imperceptible pulse can occur from the same cause.
The woman may contract with head against knees, lose sight and speech, have a distorted nose, contracted lips, clenched teeth and an unusually raised chest.

Galen's case: a woman lost pulse and voice and appeared dead; no external life sign was seen although a little heat remained near the heart. Some judged her dead. Galen placed well-carded wool at her nose and mouth and recognized life from its motion. This wool is a diagnostic object, not one of the burnt odor remedies.
The text attributes the disease to excessive corrupted seed becoming poisonous.

It singles out women without intercourse, especially widows formerly sexually active, and virgins of marriageable age unable to have intercourse; the author's account says seed accumulates and would naturally be discharged through a male.
A cold vapor from this excessive corrupted seed ascends to parts called collaterales near heart, lung and voice organs, obstructing speech.
Menstrual deficiency can also be a principal cause. When menstruation is absent and seed excessive, the disease is more troublesome and prolonged, especially in higher parts.
Moderately rub hands and feet with laurel oil.
Apply strong-smelling substances to the nose: galbanum, opoponacum, castoreum, pitch, burnt wool, burnt linen, burnt skin and asa fetida.
Anoint the vulvae inside and outside with aromatic oils/ointments: oleum muscellinum, nard oil; the text ranks a zibethum ointment above them.
These are said to attract and provoke **menstrua**. The grammatical object is not an explicitly stated womb attracted toward a pleasant smell.
Apply cups in inguine and pectine.
In the evening give diaciminum with juice of apium or nepita, or syrup of calamentum.
Alternative: castoreum, white pepper, costus, mint and apium, one drachm each; grind and mix with white or sweet wine; give two drachms in the evening.
A physician printed as Iustianus prescribes dried cumin: one drachm or two spoonfuls as a drink. Do not silently equate these measures.
He also prescribes powder from a fox's or capriolus's penis, introduced by pessary.
Boiled lovage root, ground with axungia and tied over the navel, is said to help the same condition.
If after childbirth the matrix descends too far from its place, apply previously moistened and heated oats in a bag.
It may move from its place, descend, or emerge outside through the vulva. These are distinguished descriptions, not a two-state toggle.
The author attributes this to softened nerves and abundant cold humors.
Softening/cooling is attributed to cold air entering the openings, for example direct exposure while uncovered, or sitting long on a cold stone.
A cold-water bath is another cause: it weakens the matrix, which leaves its place.
Straining in childbirth is another stated cause. The print's construction is awkward; do not repair it into a precise mechanism.
**If it descends and does not emerge**, apply aromatics to the nose: balsamum, muscus, ambra, spica, storax and the like.
In that branch, fumigate **below** with foul-smelling substances, for example burnt linen. The phrase says inferius; a precise application to the organ itself is an interpretation.
Foment the navel with wool soaked in wine and oil.
**If it has emerged**, mix aromatics with absinthium juice and anoint the belly using a feather.
Then take equal parts ruta, castoreum and arthemisia; boil in wine until two parts are consumed, then administer as a drink. The starting volume is not stated here.
Apply boiled grain in bags to belly and navel.
Then manually restore the emerged matrix to its own place; the text includes concussa, whose exact manipulation is not resolved here.
Then the woman enters water in which balaustiae, roses, pomegranate peel, galls, sumach, myrtilli, acorns, oak leaves/bark, cypress nuts and lentils have been boiled.
Then make a stupha; Galen prescribes boxwood in a pot over live coals, with the woman seated covered above it, receiving the smoke inside herself. This is distinct from the earlier foul-smell branch.
Diet is cold and astringent, without cumin, pepper or any pungency.
Fruits: coctana, mespila, sorba, sour apples and similar things.
Drink tempered wine participating in astringency.

An additional experimentum for an emerged matrix: powdered deer heart and laurel leaves, one drachm each, and myrrh, one scruple; grind, mix with wine and give to drink. The author claims the matrix will return to its place. This alternative is retained, not merged with manual replacement.
The matrix can move from its place without rising toward the spiritualia, emerging through its opening, or descending.
Signs: left-side pain, menstrual retention, distorted limbs, difficulty urinating, abdominal twisting and rumbling.
Take apium and foenumgraecum, grind with wine and give as a drink.
Alternative: powder agaricum, plantain seed and satureia; give with wine or cooked honey.

To prevent movement and hardness: deer marrow, goose fat, red wax and butter, two ounces each; add foenumgraecum and linseed, cook in water over a slow fire until fully cooked, and introduce by pessary.
The author calls this useful against several diseases of the mouth of the matrix.
